# Problem 1: Logistic Regression for Homicide Resolution

## Data Import and Cleaning
```{r p1-01-import-data}
homicide_raw =
  read_csv(
    "data/homicide-data.csv",
    na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")
  )
```

```{r p1-02-clean-data}
homicide_df =
  homicide_raw |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, state, sep = ", "),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c(
      "Dallas, TX",
      "Phoenix, AZ",
      "Kansas City, MO",
      "Tulsa, AL"
    ),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black"),
    victim_sex %in% c("Female", "Male")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White"),
    victim_sex = fct_relevel(victim_sex, "Female")
  ) |>
  select(
    city_state, resolved, victim_age,
    victim_race, victim_sex
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```


```{r p1-03-check-data}
homicide_df |>
  summarize(
    n_observations = n(),
    n_cities = n_distinct(city_state),
    n_missing_age = sum(is.na(victim_age))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

homicide_df |>
  count(victim_race, victim_sex) |>
  knitr::kable()

homicide_df |>
  count(resolved) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The homicide data were obtained from The Washington Post's public GitHub repository. 
I created a city-state identifier and a binary outcome indicating whether a homicide 
was resolved by arrest. Dallas, TX; Phoenix, AZ; Kansas City, MO; and Tulsa, 
AL were excluded as specified in the assignment. The analysis was restricted to 
Black and White victims with known sex and complete model covariates. 
Victim age was converted to a numeric variable, and female and White victims 
were selected as the reference categories.

After data cleaning, the final analytical dataset consisted of 39,362 homicide records 
across 47 cities, with no missing values for victim age. Of these cases, 
19,207 (48.8%) were resolved by arrest, while 20,155 (51.2%) were not. 
The majority of records involved Black male victims, accounting for 73.9% of the analytical sample.



## Logistic Regression for Baltimore
```{r p1-04-baltimore-model}
baltimore_df =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD")

baltimore_fit =
  baltimore_df |>
  glm(
    resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
    data = _,
    family = binomial()
  )
```

```{r p1-05-baltimore-or}
baltimore_or =
  baltimore_fit |>
  broom::tidy(
    conf.int = TRUE,
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(
    term,
    OR = estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  )

baltimore_or |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor",
      "Adjusted OR",
      "95% CI Lower",
      "95% CI Upper"
    )
  )
```

I fitted a multivariable logistic regression model for Baltimore, MD, with homicide resolution 
as the outcome and victim age, sex, and race as predictors. After adjusting for victim age 
and race, homicides involving male victims had approximately 57.4% lower odds 
of being resolved by arrest than those involving female victims 
(adjusted OR = 0.426, 95% CI: 0.324–0.558). The confidence interval did not include 1, 
indicating a statistically significant association between victim sex and homicide resolution 
in Baltimore.



## Logistic Regression Across Cities
```{r p1-06-city-models}
city_models =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(datasets = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(
      datasets,
      \(df) glm(
        resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
        data = df,
        family = binomial()
      )
    ),
    results = map(
      fits,
      \(fit) broom::tidy(
        fit,
        conf.int = TRUE,
        exponentiate = TRUE
      )
    )
  )
```


```{r p1-07-city-or}
city_or_df =
  city_models |>
  select(city_state, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(
    city_state,
    OR = estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  ) |>
  arrange(OR)

city_or_df
```

I fitted separate logistic regression models for all 47 cities using nested data frames 
and the `map()` function. Each model included victim age, sex, and race as predictors, 
with female and White victims serving as the reference categories. The model coefficients 
and confidence limits were exponentiated to obtain city-specific adjusted odds ratios 
and 95% confidence intervals comparing male victims with female victims. The results were 
then combined into a single tidy data frame and ordered by the estimated odds ratios.

As a consistency check, the Baltimore estimate obtained from the city-specific analysis 
matched the result from the individual logistic regression model 
(adjusted OR = 0.426, 95% CI: 0.324–0.558), confirming that the iterative modeling 
workflow reproduced the Baltimore result.


## Comparison of City-Specific Odds Ratios
```{r p1-08-city-or-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 13}
city_or_df |>
  mutate(
    city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = city_state, y = OR)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Odds Ratios for Homicide Resolution by City",
    subtitle = "Male versus female victims, adjusted for age and race",
    x = "City",
    y = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)"
  )

theme(
  axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
)
```

```{r p1-09-city-or-summary}
city_or_df |>
  summarize(
    n_cities = n(),
    n_or_below_one = sum(OR < 1),
    n_ci_below_one = sum(conf.high < 1),
    n_ci_above_one = sum(conf.low > 1),
    n_ci_includes_one = sum(
      conf.low <= 1 & conf.high >= 1
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Across the 47 cities included in the analysis, 41 (87.2%) had adjusted odds ratios 
below 1, suggesting that homicides involving male victims generally had lower odds 
of being resolved by arrest than those involving female victims after adjustment 
for victim age and race.

The magnitude and precision of the estimated associations varied considerably 
across cities. The adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.262 in New York, 
NY (95% CI: 0.133–0.485), to 1.767 in Albuquerque, NM (95% CI: 0.825–3.762). 
Of the 47 cities, 22 had 95% confidence intervals entirely below 1, 
while the remaining 25 had confidence intervals that included 1. 
No city had a confidence interval entirely above 1.

Overall, the results suggest a broadly consistent pattern of lower odds of 
homicide resolution for male victims, although the strength and statistical 
precision of this association varied across cities.


# Problem 2: Bootstrap Inference for Weather Data

## Data Preparation
```{r p2-01-weather-data}
data("weather_df")

weather_model_df =
  weather_df |>
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp) |>
  drop_na()
```

```{r p2-02-check-weather}
weather_model_df |>
  summarize(
    n_observations = n(),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    mean_tmin = mean(tmin),
    mean_prcp = mean(prcp)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

tibble(
  n_original = nrow(weather_df),
  n_excluded = nrow(weather_df) - nrow(weather_model_df),
  n_final = nrow(weather_model_df),
  n_missing = sum(is.na(weather_model_df))
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The Central Park weather data were obtained from the `p8105.datasets` package 
and initially contained 2,190 observations and six variables. 
Maximum daily temperature (`tmax`) was treated as the outcome, 
with minimum daily temperature (`tmin`) and precipitation (`prcp`) included 
as predictors. After excluding 19 observations with missing values in 
any of these three variables, the final analytical dataset consisted of 
2,171 complete observations.

The mean maximum and minimum daily temperatures were 17.865 and 10.096, respectively, 
and the mean precipitation was 32.810 on the original measurement scale. 
The precipitation distribution appeared right-skewed, with a median 
of zero and a mean substantially higher than the median. All three variables 
were retained on their original measurement scales for the subsequent regression 
and bootstrap analyses.


## Linear Regression Model
```{r p2-03-original-model}
weather_fit =
  weather_model_df |>
  lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = _)

weather_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r p2-04-original-r-squared}
weather_fit |>
  broom::glance() |>
  select(r.squared) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

I fitted a multiple linear regression model using maximum daily temperature 
as the outcome and minimum daily temperature and precipitation as predictors. 
Holding precipitation constant, a one-unit increase in minimum temperature 
was associated with an approximately 1.017-unit increase in expected maximum 
temperature. Holding minimum temperature constant, a one-unit increase 
in precipitation was associated with an approximately 0.006-unit decrease 
in expected maximum temperature.

The model had an R-squared of 0.941, indicating that approximately 94.1% of 
the observed variation in maximum temperature was explained by the two predictors. 
The estimates from the original dataset served as a reference for the subsequent 
bootstrap analysis.


## Bootstrap Sampling and Model Fitting
```{r p2-05-bootstrap-models}
set.seed(1)

weather_bootstrap_df =
  weather_model_df |>
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |>
  mutate(
    model_fits = map(
      strap,
      \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)
    ),
    tidy_results = map(model_fits, broom::tidy),
    glance_results = map(model_fits, broom::glance)
  )
```

```{r p2-06-extract-estimates}
weather_boot_results =
  weather_bootstrap_df |>
  select(.id, tidy_results, glance_results) |>
  unnest(glance_results) |>
  select(
    .id,
    r_squared = r.squared,
    tidy_results
  ) |>
  unnest(tidy_results) |>
  filter(term %in% c("tmin", "prcp")) |>
  select(.id, r_squared, term, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  ) |>
  mutate(
    beta_ratio = tmin / prcp
  ) |>
  select(.id, r_squared, beta_ratio)
```

```{r p2-07-check-bootstrap}
weather_boot_results |>
  summarize(
    n_bootstrap = n(),
    n_valid_r_squared = sum(is.finite(r_squared)),
    n_valid_beta_ratio = sum(is.finite(beta_ratio))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

I initially tested the bootstrap procedure using 10 samples to verify the re-sampling, 
model fitting, and result extraction workflow. I then generated 5,000 bootstrap 
samples using `modelr::bootstrap()`, with each sample containing 2,171 observations 
drawn with replacement from the original analytical dataset.

The same multiple linear regression model was fitted to each bootstrap sample 
using the `map()` function. I used `broom::glance()` to extract R-squared 
and `broom::tidy()` to obtain the regression coefficients. The ratio of the 
minimum temperature coefficient to the precipitation coefficient was calculated 
separately for each bootstrap sample.

The procedure successfully produced 5,000 finite estimates of R-squared and 5,000 
finite estimates of the coefficient ratio, with no missing or non-finite results. 
These estimates were retained for examining the empirical bootstrap distributions 
and constructing 95% percentile confidence intervals.



## Bootstrap Distributions
```{r p2-08-bootstrap-long}
weather_boot_long =
  weather_boot_results |>
  rename(
    "R-squared" = r_squared,
    "Coefficient ratio" = beta_ratio
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -.id,
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  )
```

```{r p2-09-bootstrap-density, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
weather_boot_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distributions of Regression Quantities",
    subtitle = "Based on 5,000 bootstrap samples",
    x = "Bootstrap estimate",
    y = "Density"
  )
```

The bootstrap distribution of R-squared was approximately bell-shaped with 
slight negative skewness and was tightly concentrated around 0.941, suggesting that 
the proportion of variation explained by the model was relatively stable across 
the 5,000 bootstrap samples.

In contrast, the bootstrap distribution of the coefficient ratio was noticeably 
left-skewed, with a peak around −170 and a long tail extending toward more 
negative values. This asymmetry may be attributable to the relatively 
small magnitude of the precipitation coefficient in the denominator, 
making the ratio sensitive to small changes in its estimate across bootstrap samples.

These empirical distributions illustrate how sampling uncertainty can differ 
between regression quantities. In particular, the asymmetry of the coefficient 
ratio distribution highlights the usefulness of bootstrap percentile confidence 
intervals, which do not require a normal approximation to the sampling distribution.



## Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
```{r p2-10-bootstrap-ci}
weather_boot_ci =
  weather_boot_long |>
  group_by(quantity) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate),
    bootstrap_se = sd(estimate),
    ci_lower = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    ci_upper = quantile(estimate, 0.975)
  )

weather_boot_ci |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Quantity",
      "Bootstrap Mean",
      "Bootstrap SE",
      "95% CI Lower",
      "95% CI Upper"
    )
  )
```

Based on the 5,000 bootstrap samples, the mean estimate of R-squared was 0.941, 
with a bootstrap standard error of 0.003 and a 95% percentile confidence interval 
of (0.934, 0.947). The relatively narrow confidence interval suggests that 
the proportion of variation in maximum temperature explained by the regression model 
was stable across the resampled datasets.

The mean estimate of the coefficient ratio was −185.024, with a bootstrap 
standard error of 38.551 and a 95% percentile confidence interval 
of (−274.795, −125.484). The asymmetry of this interval is consistent 
with the left-skewed bootstrap distribution observed in the preceding density plot.

Both confidence intervals were constructed using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles 
of their respective empirical bootstrap distributions. These findings demonstrate 
the usefulness of bootstrapping for quantifying uncertainty in regression 
quantities, particularly when their sampling distributions are asymmetric 
or difficult to derive analytically.

# Problem 3: Birthweight Regression and Cross Validation

## Data Import and Cleaning
```{r p3-01-birthweight-import}
birthweight_raw =
  read_csv("data/birthweight.csv")
```

```{r p3-02-birthweight-clean}
birthweight_df =
  birthweight_raw |>
  mutate(
    babysex = factor(
      babysex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    frace = factor(
      frace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9),
      labels = c(
        "White", "Black", "Asian",
        "Puerto Rican", "Other", "Unknown"
      )
    ),
    mrace = factor(
      mrace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8),
      labels = c(
        "White", "Black", "Asian",
        "Puerto Rican", "Other"
      )
    ),
    malform = factor(
      malform,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Absent", "Present")
    )
  )
```

```{r p3-03-birthweight-validation}
birthweight_df |>
  summarize(
    n_observations = n(),
    n_variables = ncol(birthweight_df),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(birthweight_df))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

birthweight_df |>
  count(babysex) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The birthweight dataset was imported from a local CSV file and contained 4,342 
observations and 20 variables. Infant sex, maternal race, paternal race, 
and the presence of congenital malformations were converted from numeric 
codes to categorical variables according to the definitions provided in the assignment. 
Male infants, White parents, and the absence of congenital malformations were 
set as the respective reference categories. All remaining quantitative variables 
were retained in their original numeric form.

No missing values were identified after recoding, so all 4,342 observations 
were retained for subsequent analysis. The dataset included 2,230 male 
infants (51.4%) and 2,112 female infants (48.6%). Congenital malformations 
were uncommon, with only 15 infants (0.35%) recorded as having malformations.

## Proposed Regression Model
```{r p3-04-model-data}
birthweight_model_df =
  birthweight_df |>
  select(
    bwt, bhead, blength, gaweeks,
    babysex, ppwt, wtgain, smoken
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```

I developed a multiple linear regression model based on a hypothesized set of factors 
associated with birthweight. The model included infant head circumference, 
birth length, gestational age, and sex, as well as maternal pre-pregnancy weight, 
gestational weight gain, and smoking during pregnancy.

These predictors were selected to capture infant size, pregnancy duration, 
and maternal characteristics relevant to fetal growth. Rather than relying 
on an automated variable-selection procedure, I prioritized a reasonably 
parsimonious and interpretable model. The primary objective was to 
predict birthweight using information available at delivery rather than 
to estimate causal effects.


```{r p3-05-proposed-model}
proposed_fit =
  birthweight_model_df |>
  lm(
    bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + babysex +
      ppwt + wtgain + smoken,
    data = _
  )

proposed_fit |>
  broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(
    term, estimate, conf.low,
    conf.high, p.value
  ) |>
  mutate(
    p.value = if_else(
      p.value < 0.001,
      "<0.001",
      as.character(round(p.value, 3))
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The proposed multiple linear regression model was fitted using all 4,342 observations. 
After adjusting for the other predictors, greater head circumference, birth length, 
gestational age, maternal pre-pregnancy weight, and gestational weight gain 
were associated with higher expected birthweight.

Holding all other predictors constant, a one-centimeter increase in head 
circumference was associated with an approximately 136.6-gram increase 
in expected birthweight (95% CI: 129.7–143.5), while a one-centimeter 
increase in birth length was associated with a 78.3-gram increase 
(95% CI: 74.3–82.4). Maternal smoking was negatively associated with birthweight, 
with each additional cigarette smoked per day corresponding to an approximately 
2.2-gram decrease in expected birthweight (95% CI: −3.3 to −1.1). 
Female infants had an estimated birthweight 31.0 grams higher than male 
infants after adjustment for the other predictors.

The model had an R-squared and adjusted R-squared of approximately 0.699, 
indicating that it explained 69.9% of the observed variation in birthweight. 
Although the model showed a reasonably good fit to the observed data, residual 
diagnostics and cross-validation were needed to assess model adequacy and 
predictive performance on held-out observations.


## Residual Diagnostics
```{r p3-06-residual-plot}
birthweight_model_df |>
  modelr::add_predictions(proposed_fit) |>
  modelr::add_residuals(proposed_fit) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals versus Fitted Birthweight",
    x = "Fitted birthweight (grams)",
    y = "Residuals (grams)"
  )
```

The residuals were generally centered around zero, particularly within the range 
where most fitted birthweights were concentrated. However, the residual plot showed 
some systematic patterns at lower fitted values and variation in residual spread 
across the range of predictions, suggesting possible departures from the linearity 
and constant variance assumptions.

Several observations had relatively large residuals, particularly positive residuals 
exceeding 2,000 grams, indicating that the model substantially underestimated 
birthweight for some infants. A small number of fitted birthweights were also 
negative, which is physiologically implausible and highlights a limitation of 
the linear regression model at the lower end of the prediction range.

Although the proposed model explained approximately 69.9% of the observed 
variation in birthweight, the residual diagnostics suggest that its fit was 
not equally adequate across all observations. The model was retained for 
comparison with the two alternative models using cross-validated prediction error.

## Alternative Regression Models
```{r p3-07-alternative-models}
main_effects_fit =
  birthweight_model_df |>
  lm(
    bwt ~ blength + gaweeks,
    data = _
  )

interaction_fit =
  birthweight_model_df |>
  lm(
    bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex,
    data = _
  )
```
The proposed model was compared with two alternative regression models specified 
in the assignment. The first alternative included birth length and gestational 
age as main effects only. The second included head circumference, birth length, 
infant sex, and all corresponding two-way and three-way interactions. 
These three candidate models were subsequently evaluated using cross-validated 
prediction error.


## Monte Carlo Cross Validation
```{r p3-08-cv-splits}
set.seed(1)

cv_df =
  crossv_mc(birthweight_model_df, 100) |>
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble),
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )
```

```{r p3-09-cv-models}
cv_df =
  cv_df |>
  mutate(
    proposed_fit = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(
        bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + babysex +
          ppwt + wtgain + smoken,
        data = df
      )
    ),
    main_effects_fit = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(
        bwt ~ blength + gaweeks,
        data = df
      )
    ),
    interaction_fit = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(
        bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex,
        data = df
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r p3-10-cv-rmse}
cv_df =
  cv_df |>
  mutate(
    rmse_proposed = map2_dbl(
      proposed_fit, test, rmse
    ),
    rmse_main_effects = map2_dbl(
      main_effects_fit, test, rmse
    ),
    rmse_interaction = map2_dbl(
      interaction_fit, test, rmse
    )
  )
```

I evaluated the predictive performance of the three candidate models using 100 Monte
Carlo cross-validation splits. In each iteration, approximately 80% of the dataset
(3,473 observations) was assigned to training and 20% (869 observations) to testing. 
The same training and testing datasets were used for all three models within each 
iteration to ensure a fair comparison.

Each model was fitted to the training data using the `map()` function, and 
its predictive performance was evaluated on the corresponding held-out testing 
data using root mean squared error (RMSE). The `map2_dbl()` function was used to 
pair each fitted model with its corresponding testing dataset.

All 100 cross-validation iterations successfully produced finite RMSE estimates 
for each of the three models, yielding a total of 300 testing RMSE values. 
These estimates were used to examine the distribution of prediction errors 
and compare predictive performance across the three candidate models.


## Comparison of Prediction Error
```{r p3-11-rmse-long}
birthweight_rmse_long =
  cv_df |>
  select(.id, starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("rmse_"),
    names_to = "model",
    names_prefix = "rmse_",
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model = fct_inorder(model)
  )
```

```{r p3-12-rmse-plot}
birthweight_rmse_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c(
      proposed = "Proposed",
      main_effects = "Main effects",
      interaction = "Interaction"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Cross-Validated Prediction Error for Birthweight Models",
    subtitle = "Based on 100 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits",
    x = "Regression model",
    y = "Testing RMSE (grams)"
  )
```

```{r p3-13-rmse-summary}
rmse_summary =
  birthweight_rmse_long |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
    median_rmse = median(rmse),
    sd_rmse = sd(rmse)
  ) |>
  arrange(mean_rmse)

rmse_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c(
      "Model",
      "Mean RMSE",
      "Median RMSE",
      "SD of RMSE"
    )
  )
```

Across the 100 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits, the proposed model achieved 
the lowest mean testing RMSE (281.33 grams), followed by the interaction 
model (288.60 grams) and the main-effects model (332.23 grams). 
The proposed model reduced the mean prediction error by approximately 
50.90 grams compared with the main-effects model and by 7.27 grams 
compared with the interaction model.

The violin plot showed that the main-effects model generally had higher prediction 
errors and greater variability across the cross-validation splits. In contrast, 
the RMSE distributions of the proposed and interaction models overlapped 
considerably, suggesting that the improvement offered by the proposed model 
over the interaction model was relatively modest. The proposed model also had 
the lowest standard deviation of RMSE (8.36 grams), indicating relatively 
consistent predictive performance across the repeated data splits.

Overall, the proposed model, which incorporated infant measurements, gestational age, 
and maternal characteristics, provided the best predictive performance among the 
three candidate models. Although the residual diagnostics identified some 
limitations, particularly at lower fitted birthweights, the cross-validation 
results supported the proposed model as the preferred model for prediction 
within this dataset.
